newsitem.title: USA: Dlr dips after U.S. open amid ambiguous jobs data.
newsitem.headline: Dlr dips after U.S. open amid ambiguous jobs data.

text.p: The dollar opened slightly above Thursday's closing levels, then slumped against European currencies after a report showing confusing signals in the U.S. labor market.
While nonfarm payrolls rose a modest 142,000 in April and average hourly earnings fell for the first time in six months, the jobless rate fell to a 23-year low.

Market players focused on the soft payrolls, which analysts had forecast to rise by 211,000, and the implications for lower inflation in the wage data. Both numbers suggest the Federal Reserve could delay interest rate hikes, dealers said.
"The payrolls number was lower than anticipated and the dollar came off a bit," said Bill Bertha, chief dealer at Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh.
Dealers also cited an article in Businessweek magazine for downward pressure on the greenback. The story suggested the Fed may not have to raise rates again this spring.

The dollar opened at 1.7235/45 marks, up from 1.7220/25 at Thursday's close. Shortly after the jobs data, the dollar slipped below 1.72 marks. Dollar/Swiss opened lower at 1.4685/95 from 1.4695/05 before slipping to a session low at 1.4655.

Dollar/Swiss may have been hurt by comments by Swiss National Bank board member Bruno Gehrig, dealers said. Gehrig in a speech warned against excessive loosening of monetary policy, which would lead to "rapidly rising interest rates."
Dollar/yen opened slightly higher at 126.66/71 versus 126.55/60 and held steady after the jobs report.
A drop in the British pound highlighted overnight trading amid concerns of weak-pound policies in the wake of the huge election victory by the UK's Labor party.
Speculation grew after a London Times editorial discussed possible sterling devaluation, traders said.
"In the past, Labor has relied on devaluation in the currency. I think it's kind of a bogus dynamic, but I understand some U.S. funds were sellers of sterling," said one trader.

But with Labor's incoming Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown to meet Bank of England Governor Eddie George next Wednesday, market players wondered aloud whether the pair would agree on a much-anticipated hike in interest rates.
"I'm pretty confident of a quarter-point hike, but no more," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group, Ltd in Chicago.
Sterling slumped broadly overnight, before steadying and remained under pressure in morning U.S. trade.
Gains by the mark and Swiss franc versus the pound contributed to the weakness in dollar/Europe, traders said.
"Sterling is going pretty soft right now, particularly against the European currencies. That might keep the dollar under pressure," Bertha said.

But the dollar's biggest threat now appears to be any sign of economic or inflationary moderation in the United States, traders said. Any hint of narrowing yield differentials currently favoring the dollar could cause dollar selling.
"Lately we have been trading on interest differentials, which had been getting wider so you just needed to hold dollars in order to get a return," said Russell LaScala, chief dealer at Citibank.
Elsewhere, the dollar opened lower at Canadian $1.3841/46 from C$1.3871/76. The Australian dollar opened at $0.7838/43.
The pound opened at $1.6108/18, down from $1.6235/45.
((--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664))
